entry.title: Ark (Part-2)
entry.content:
Ark Series  —  ← Part 1: Not Every Token Deserves Softmax  |  Part 2: Results  |  Part 3: Kernels and Systems →

In Part 1 we built Ark: a single block in which a learned router sends each entry (one token, in one KV group, of one layer) either to a KV cache read with the exponential kernel, or to a fixed-size recurrent state read with the linear kernel. Ark keeps only about 10% of entries in the KV cache, so the central question is simple:

Does storing so little cost quality?

Short answer: not much. On recall, Ark is competitive with Transformers and with strong hybrids while storing about a tenth of a Transformer’s memory and 25–53% less than the hybrids.

Setup

We train Ark at ~400M, ~800M and ~2B parameters (on 15B, 32B and 200B tokens), keeping about 10% of entries in the KV cache. We compare it with Transformers (RoPE, NoPE, FoX, and MLA at the smaller scales) and with hybrids that interleave NoPE softmax layers with GLA or Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, where \(1{:}x\) means one softmax block per \(x\) recurrent blocks. Memory is counted as stored elements, recurrent state plus KV cache, at 8K context, so very different architectures share one axis.

Recall with Less Memory

Single-fact recall. We start at all three scales: extracting a value from a document (SWDE, FDA), answering reading-comprehension questions (SQuAD), and finding a needle in a haystack at 2K–8K context (NIAH-1 to NIAH-3, the hardest with a UUID as the needle).

Ark keeps pace with the best hybrids while storing 25–53% less. At 2B it lands within about a point of GDN 1:6 on SWDE, FDA and SQuAD, and at 800M it beats it on all three. It is also the model to beat on the hardest needle, a UUID hidden at 4K context: at both 400M and 800M Ark finds it best, while several baselines collapse.

Ark’s main gap is the UUID needle at 8K, where the 2B GDN hybrids lead. We hypothesize the cause is the decay, not the routing: we gave Ark the simplest and cheapest one, a single scalar per step, while GDN’s delta rule can also erase along the incoming key. Since the router doesn’t care what recurrence sits underneath, a richer one can be swapped in, which we leave for future work.

Long-context RULER tasks. RULER’s basic single-needle tasks (NIAH-1 to NIAH-3) are already in the recall tables above. The extended 2B suite from RULER and BABILong goes beyond one fact per query, with variable tracking, word aggregation, multi-hop QA and multi-item retrieval at 2K–8K context.

On aggregation and QA, Ark is the strongest model in the suite, and it does so with the smallest memory of any. It leads at every length on frequent-word extraction, SQuAD-based QA and BABILong, and beats every hybrid on multi-key NIAH with a single target.

Its limit shows when one query needs many tokens back exactly: multiple queries, the harder multi-key variants, and multiple values at 8K. There the strongest hybrids and Transformers pull ahead. Ark keeps only about 10% of its entries exactly, so those tokens compete for the same space; a budget that adapts to the input is the natural next step.

Learning What to Keep

Ark decides during training which entries to keep. Is that better than the simpler alternatives?

Against KV eviction. There is another way to get a small cache: train a full Transformer and evict entries at inference time. We compare Ark against four training-free policies, StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV and AdaKV, applied to RoPE, NoPE and FoX Transformers. To make the baseline as strong as possible, we take the best score in each column separately over all eleven combinationsFoX omits AdaKV because per-head retained sets are incompatible with its GPU decoding kernel., a baseline stronger than any real eviction policy, and give it at least as much memory as Ark.

Against content-agnostic routing. Does the router’s choice of which entries to keep matter, or only the size of the cache? We replace the learned router with two allocations that ignore content: random, which retains each entry independently with the target probability, and periodic, which retains an evenly spaced fraction.

At equal memory, Ark outperforms even this per-task best policy on nearly every task, often by a wide margin. At 800M, it nearly doubles FDA accuracy (81.3 vs. 41.9), and it keeps near-perfect UUID retrieval at 4K, where eviction collapses. The difference is when the choice is made. An evicting model is trained expecting to see every token and only loses some at inference. Ark is trained with the choice built in: it learns which tokens deserve the cache, and the ones it lets go still live on, compressed, in the recurrent state.

At a matched ~10% budget, the learned router improves extraction accuracy 1.8–4.7×, and it is the only policy that reliably finds the UUID needle. Even with 4.6× as many KV entries, random routing recovers the easier needles but still trails the learned router on the UUID needle and extraction.

The recall comes from choosing the right tokens, not from the size of the cache.

Ablations

How many teacher queries?

The approximation loss from Part 1 compares the routed attention distribution against the softmax teacher on \(\lvert\mathcal Q\rvert\) sampled query positions per sequence, at cost \(O(\lvert\mathcal Q\rvert T)\) per head. How many do we need?

\(\lvert\mathcal Q\rvert\) 0 1 5 10 20 60 200
Realized compression (%) 99.76 89.42 89.57 89.66 89.34 89.25 89.55
Val. PPL ↓ 13.86 12.64 12.63 12.65 12.65 12.63 12.65
SWDE 11.2 51.6 50.9 53.8 49.0 53.9 50.9
FDA 2.0 68.8 66.6 71.9 69.9 63.2 63.5
SQuAD 19.3 29.8 32.1 30.5 33.6 34.0 31.9

With \(\lvert\mathcal Q\rvert=0\) the budget is the only signal, and the router collapses to compressing nearly every entry (99.76%), which hurts both perplexity and recall. A single sampled query per sequence prevents the collapse. More queries help only mildly, mainly on SQuAD, so we use 10 and supervision stays cheap.

Architecture choices

The Ark block uses (i) a \(1+\mathrm{elu}\) feature map, the best of those we tried (\(\exp\) is the weakest); (ii) QK-RMSNorm in each branch, worth 14 points of mean recall; (iii) LoRA only on the linear branch, before the norm; (iv) no short convolution, which hurts recall wherever we place it; and (v) decay in every layer, since NoPE layers help some retrieval tasks but hurt others.

Choice (iv) might be seen as against common practice, since almost every modern linear model relies on a short convolution as a crutch for retrieval. But a model that stores exact tokens can retrieve them directly: attention never needed a convolution, and neither does Raven. The same goes for Ark, which keeps the tokens that matter exactly.

How Ark Uses Its Two Memories

Ark is trained to keep retrieval-relevant entries in the KV cache. But does the trained model actually rely on them? We override the routing of a trained 400M model at inference time, without changing any weights.

Experiment 1: force every entry into one memory, either all into the KV cache or all into the recurrent state.

Experiment 2: move only the answer tokens. We locate every occurrence of the answer in the context and force just those tokens to the linear kernel, in every layer and KV group. Everything else keeps its learned routing decision.

The ~10% of entries in the KV cache carry nearly all of the model’s retrieval ability. With everything in the recurrent state, commonsense tasks barely notice, while retrieval and long-range prediction collapse, down to 0% on FDA. This matches what we found in Transformers: retrieval runs through exact attention on only a few positions.

Keeping everything in the KV cache does not restore retrieval either; it roughly halves FDA and SWDE accuracy. The trained model depends on the KV cache for retained entries and on the recurrent state for the rest. The recurrent state does real work of its own, not just catching what the cache drops.

In Experiment 2, mean accuracy drops from 52.1% to 8.4%. Retrieval fails not because the cache got smaller, but because the specific entries it needed are gone. It’s the same lesson as the routing ablation, seen from the other side: what matters is which tokens are kept.

What Does the Router Keep?

Below is one KV group of a trained Ark model: blue tokens are kept in the KV cache and orange tokens are folded into the recurrent state. Only about 13% of tokens are cached, and most of them are punctuation marks at sentence boundaries, along with fragments of the codes hidden in the text. By caching at the punctuation, Ark learns on its own a coarser abstraction of the input: the sentence rather than the single token. This is close in spirit to H-Net, where the model learns from data how large a unit of input to abstract over and store.

The periods surprised us. We expected every layer to spend its cache on retrieval. Instead, some heads cache the end of each sentence, probably condensing what the sentence said into that one token, while other heads do the retrieval. In hindsight this mirrors the gather heads of gather-and-aggregate, which condense a span into a single token that other heads can later retrieve.

In the NIAH task below an 8K-token prompt streams through one router (layer 20, KV group 3), and its score is plotted as each token arrives. Across the haystack the score stays low and almost everything goes to the recurrent state; when the needle arrives, the score jumps above the threshold and the needle’s tokens are kept in the KV cache.

No one told the router what a needle is. It learned, from the softmax teacher and a budget (Part 1), that a few positions carry information the recurrent state cannot hold, and it spends its cache there. Experiment 2 confirms it: without those tokens in the KV cache, retrieval collapses.

Up Next

A smaller footprint only matters if it turns into speed. In Part 3 we walk through the algorithms behind both branches, a packed-attention kernel for the exponential branch and a log-space chunked recurrence for the linear branch, and how Ark ends up decoding 3.35× faster than FlashAttention and 1.60× faster than a GLA hybrid at 64K context.

entry.title: Ark (Part-1)
entry.content:
Ark Series  —  Part 1: Not Every Token Deserves Softmax  |  Part 2: Results →  |  Part 3: Kernels and Systems →

🚢 An ark can’t carry everything through the flood, so it has to choose what comes aboard. A language model reading a long context faces its own flood of tokens: caching every one makes memory grow with the context, while compressing all of them into a fixed-size state blurs the details it may later need to recall.

Attention Routing Kernels (Ark) take the ark’s approach. Ark is a new attention layer that decides, token by token, what to keep exactly in a KV cache and what to compress into a recurrent state. Across 400M–2B parameters it is competitive with Transformers and hybrid models while storing a fraction of their memory, and at 64K context it decodes 3.35× faster than FlashAttention.

How Much Attention Do We Need?

Recurrent models fold each token into a fixed-size state, so they run in linear time with constant memory, yet they still trail Transformers on recall. The go-to fix today is the hybrid: interleave a few softmax attention layers among many recurrent ones. Recent large-scale releases such as Kimi K3, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 are all built this way.

Why does a little attention go so far? Recurrent models fall furthest behind on tasks that hinge on retrieval, finding and reusing something given earlier in the prompt. Looking inside the models showed why: both Transformers and recurrent models implement retrieval with the same two-step circuit, termed gather-and-aggregate (G&A). It lives in only a few heads, and recurrent models run it less sharply; swapping even one of them for attention brings the recurrent model closer to the Transformer. That is what the attention layers of a hybrid provide.

But hybrids keep far more exact memory than retrieval needs: every attention layer caches every token, at a ratio set by hand. Retrieval-aware distillation (RAD) keeps only G&A heads as attention (2% of the overall heads) and distills the rest into recurrent heads, recovering over 95% of the teacher on retrieval-heavy tasks. Each head RAD keeps still caches every token, though retrieval needs only a few, and which ones depends on the input. The last step is to choose per token, and to learn that choice during training.

Can a single layer learn, token by token, what to cache and what to compress into its recurrent state?

We think this is where next-generation architectures should go: not a stack of separate attention and recurrent layers, but one kind of layer that holds both memories and learns the pattern of what to compress. In effect, the network learns its own architecture, placing each head anywhere between attention and recurrence. Its KV cache grows only with the tokens worth remembering exactly, next to a compact state that absorbs everything else. That is what we built Ark for.

Two Kernels, Two Memories

Every autoregressive sequence model has to decide how the current token reads the past. Write the queries, keys and values as \(q_t, k_t, v_t\). Causal attention is a weighted average over past values, and the weights come from a similarity kernel:

\[o_t = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^t \mathrm{sim}(q_t, k_j)\, v_j}{\sum_{j=1}^t \mathrm{sim}(q_t, k_j)}.\]

Choosing the kernel decides much more than the weights. It decides what the model has to remember.

The exponential kernel needs a KV cache

Softmax attention uses the exponential kernel \(\mathrm{sim}(q,k)=\exp(q^\top k)\) (with \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) absorbed into \(q\)). This kernel does not factorize: there is no finite feature map that turns \(\exp(q^\top k)\) into an inner product. To evaluate the sum for every new query, the model has to keep every past key and value around. That is the KV cache. It grows linearly with context, and its size dominates long-context inference memory.

The linear kernel folds into a state

Linear attention uses a kernel that does factorize, \(\mathrm{sim}(q,k)=\phi(q)^\top\phi(k)\), with a non-negative feature map \(\phi\). Then the sums can be accumulated ahead of time:

\[o_t = \frac{\phi(q_t)^\top S_t}{\phi(q_t)^\top z_t}, \qquad S_t = \sum_{j\le t}\phi(k_j)\,v_j^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v},\quad z_t = \sum_{j\le t}\phi(k_j).\]

The whole history lives in a fixed-size recurrent state \((S_t, z_t)\). It is cheap to carry, but individual tokens are blended together and cannot be recovered exactly. That is why recurrent models struggle with recall.

One shared notion of position

So far, both kernels compare only content; neither knows how far back a key is. Transformers usually inject position through positional embeddings, and today’s standard choice is rotary embeddings (RoPE), which rotate queries and keys by position-dependent angles so that each score depends on the relative distance. That suits the exponential kernel, but Ark needs one positional scheme that works for both kernels, and RoPE is awkward for the linear one: once the non-negative features \(\phi(q),\phi(k)\) are rotated, a score can turn negative and the normalizing sum can even hit zero. A cleaner option is temporal decay, which works for both kernels and is what the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) uses in softmax attention. A forget gate \(f_u\in(0,1)\), which doubles as a positional encoding (see our post On the Legacy of Linear Transformers in Positional Embeddings), multiplies every score by

\[f_{j:t} = \prod_{u=j+1}^{t} f_u ,\]

and for the linear kernel this keeps the recurrence: \(S_t = f_t S_{t-1} + \phi(k_t)v_t^\top\). Because the same decay applies to both kernels, a token’s positional weight does not depend on which memory it ends up in. This will matter a lot when we route.

Attention Routing Kernels

Ark chooses the kernel separately for each entry. An entry assigned to the exponential kernel stays in the KV cache. An entry assigned to the linear kernel is folded into the recurrent state. Every query reads both memories.

One router, two memories

The choice is made by a learned router \(r:\mathcal X\to\lbrace 0,1\rbrace\) that looks only at the token’s own representation \(x_j\). With \(r(x_j)=1\) the entry is retained: it stays in the KV cache and is read through the exponential (softmax) kernel. With \(r(x_j)=0\) it is compressed: it is folded into the recurrent state and read through the linear kernel. The router commits when a token is written, without ever seeing the queries that will later look it up. In return, routing stays causal, and at decode time each new token goes straight into one memory and stays there.

Formally, let \(R(t)=\lbrace j\le t : r(x_j)=1\rbrace\) be the retained set. Splitting the decayed attention sum by routing decision gives a linear part over the compressed entries and a softmax part over the retained ones:

\[o_t = \frac{\textcolor{#D9730D}{\phi(q_t)^\top S_t} \;+\; \textcolor{#2E6DB4}{\sum_{j\in R(t)} \exp(q_t^\top k_j)\,f_{j:t}\,v_j}} {\textcolor{#D9730D}{\phi(q_t)^\top z_t} \;+\; \textcolor{#2E6DB4}{\sum_{j\in R(t)} \exp(q_t^\top k_j)\,f_{j:t}}},\]

where the recurrent state now only accumulates the entries assigned to the linear kernel:

\[{S_t = f_t S_{t-1} + (1-r(x_t))\,\phi(k_t)v_t^\top, \qquad z_t = f_t z_{t-1} + (1-r(x_t))\,\phi(k_t).}\]

The output combines a cheap linear (recurrent) part with an expressive softmax part over the retained set, under one shared normalizer: unlike in a hybrid, the two kernels compete for the same attention mass inside a single layer. So a query reads from the cache and the state in proportion to their summed scores, with their magnitudes on one scale. When the query finds a strong match in the cache, the cache scores dominate; when it doesn’t, the state scores do. And since both parts share the decay \(f_{j:t}\), a token fades with distance at the same rate whichever memory holds it; routing only changes how its content is matched against a query.

Why decide at write time, and not per query? Sparse-attention methods such as NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention pick, for every query, which past tokens to read. With context length \(L\) and \(K \ll L\) selected tokens, each query’s attention costs \(O(K)\) instead of \(O(L)\), so a full sequence costs \(O(LK)\) rather than \(O(L^2)\) (DSA still runs a lightweight indexer over all \(L\) tokens to make the choice). That is flexible and saves compute, but every token has to stay in the KV cache in case a later query selects it, so the cache still holds \(O(L)\) entries: sparse readout reduces computation, not the linearly growing memory. Ark makes one fixed, causal and cheap decision per token, once, and a compressed token never enters the cache at all. The cache grows only with the retained set \(R(t)\), about a tenth of the tokens at our budget, while everything else lives in a fixed-size state. That is what actually cuts memory.

Why does the router see only the token itself? Looking only at \(x_j\) keeps decoding simple: one decision when a token arrives, no lookahead and no revisiting. The flip side is that a token whose importance only becomes clear later cannot be recovered exactly once it is compressed. A router that can revisit its decisions, or a budget that adapts to the input, is the natural next step; we come back to it at the end of Part 3.

Routing splits the attention matrix in two

The router sees only the token itself, so once an entry picks a kernel, every later query in that KV group reads it through that kernel. In the score matrix, routing colors whole columns. Here is the readout for five tokens with routing \(r=[1,0,1,0,0]\): tokens 1 and 3 are retained and read through the exponential kernel, and the rest are compressed and read through the linear kernel.

Because routing colors whole columns, the readout splits exactly into two smaller problems. Gather the blue columns and you get a packed problem: every query attends only to the retained keys \(k_1, k_3\), so the score matrix shrinks from \(5\times 5\) to \(5\times 2\) and only \(v_1, v_3\) need to sit in the KV cache. The orange columns form a recurrent problem: a causal linear-attention readout over \(k_2, k_4, k_5\), which never has to be materialized because it folds into the state \((S_t, z_t)\). The readout above is exactly the sum of the two (decay and the shared normalizer are left out for clarity):

The two parts meet only in the shared normalizer, so each can run on its own kernel: exponential attention over the packed retained entries, and a linear recurrence over everything else. This split is what makes Ark cheap, and Part 3 shows how each side is implemented.

Two familiar models are special cases. With \(r\equiv 1\), everything is retained and Ark is softmax attention with a forget gate (FoX). With \(r\equiv 0\), everything is compressed and Ark is decayed linear attention. Ark lives in between and lets the data decide where.

The Ark Block

Building an Ark model is simple: unlike a hybrid, it stacks a single type of layer, an Ark block followed by a gated MLP, each wrapped in an RMSNorm and a residual connection. The router decides where memory goes, so there is no layer ratio to tune.

Inside the block, the input is projected into a router score, a decay gate, values, and queries and keys. The router sends each token either to the KV cache, read through the exponential kernel, or into the recurrent state, read through the linear kernel, and every query reads both under one shared normalizer. The output then goes through an RMSNorm, a swish gate and the output projection.

The two kernels share their base query and key projections, but the best key for exact retrieval is not the best input to the linear kernel’s feature map, here \(\phi(x)=1+\mathrm{elu}(x)\), so the linear kernel adds small low-rank adapters (QK LoRA) on top. Each kernel also RMS-normalizes its own queries and keys so their scores stay comparable in the shared normalizer. There is no short convolution: it hurt recall in our ablations.

Teaching the Router

The router has a hard job: it must decide whether a token will need exact recall before the query that needs it arrives. We give it that signal with two simple losses. The first uses full softmax attention as a teacher: a token should stay in the KV cache if reading it through the linear kernel would noticeably change the attention distribution that the softmax kernel would have produced. We only need to check this on a handful of randomly sampled queries per sequence, so it is cheap. The second is a budget: on its own, the teacher would happily keep everything, so we ask each sequence to compress at least about 90% of its entries. The budget only says how much to compress, pooled over all layers and KV groups, never where, so the router is free to spend its cache wherever retrieval needs it.

These losses train only the router; the rest of the model is trained by the usual language-modeling loss.

Deep dive: the two router losses

The router is a linear score per layer \(\ell\) and KV group \(g\), thresholded at \(\tau\):

\[\tilde r_{\ell g}(x_t) = \sigma\!\left(W_R^{(\ell,g)} x_t\right), \qquad r_{\ell g}(x_t) = \mathbf 1\!\left[\tilde r_{\ell g}(x_t) > \tau\right], \qquad \mathcal L_{\text{router}} = \lambda_{\text{approx}}\mathcal L_{\text{approx}} + \lambda_{\text{budget}}\mathcal L_{\text{budget}} .\]

Approximation loss (the softmax teacher). For a query \(t\), define the branch-normalized distributions

\[\textcolor{#2E6DB4}{P^{\exp}_{tj} = \frac{\exp(q_t^\top k_j)f_{j:t}}{\sum_{u\le t}\exp(q_t^\top k_u)f_{u:t}}}, \qquad \textcolor{#D9730D}{P^{\text{lin}}_{tj} = \frac{\phi(q_t)^\top\phi(k_j)f_{j:t}}{\sum_{u\le t}\phi(q_t)^\top\phi(k_u)f_{u:t}}} .\]

The hard decision is not differentiable, so we mix the two with the router score and renormalize, \(\widetilde P_t \propto \textcolor{#2E6DB4}{\tilde r_j P^{\exp}_{tj}} + \textcolor{#D9730D}{(1-\tilde r_j)P^{\text{lin}}_{tj}}\), and compare it to the teacher on a small set \(\mathcal Q\) of uniformly sampled queries:

\[\mathcal L_{\text{approx}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal Q|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal Q}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\textcolor{#2E6DB4}{P^{\exp}_t} \,\big\|\, \widetilde P_t\right).\]

This is an unbiased estimate of the average over all queries. We use \(\lvert\mathcal Q\rvert = 10\); Part 2 shows that even a single sampled query per sequence is enough.

Budget loss. With a target linear fraction \(\textcolor{#D9730D}{c^{\ast}_{\text{lin}}}=0.9\) and the realized fraction \(\textcolor{#D9730D}{\bar c_{\text{lin},b}}\) of sequence \(b\), pooled over all its layers, KV groups and positions, we penalize only a shortfall:

\[\mathcal L_{\text{budget}} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\max\!\left(\textcolor{#D9730D}{c^{\ast}_{\text{lin}}} - \textcolor{#D9730D}{\bar c_{\text{lin},b}},\, 0\right)^2 .\]

The forward pass uses the hard indicator with a straight-through estimator. The weight \(\lambda_{\text{budget}}\) adapts online, growing while a batch compresses too little and shrinking once it compresses enough, so the budget is a soft training target rather than a hard cap at inference.

What Comes Next

  • In Part 2, we look at the results: recall, long-context RULER tasks, comparisons against KV eviction at equal memory, and ablations that show which tokens are kept matters more than how many.
  • In Part 3, we open up the systems side: the packed-attention kernel for the exponential branch, the log-space chunked recurrence for the linear branch, how they merge, and how all of this turns into a 3.35× decoding speedup at 64K context.

entry.title: Ark (Part-3)
entry.content:
Ark Series  —  ← Part 1: Not Every Token Deserves Softmax  |  ← Part 2: Results  |  Part 3: Kernels and Systems

Part 2 showed that Ark stores far less than Transformers and hybrids at similar quality. That smaller memory also buys speed: at 64K context, Ark decodes 3.35× faster than FlashAttention and 1.60× faster than a GLA hybrid. Here, we walk through the algorithms and optimizations behind those numbers, all implemented as Triton kernels. Recall the routed output from Part 1, with retained set \(R(t)\) and decay \(f_{j:t}=\prod_{u=j+1}^{t} f_u\):

\[o_t = \frac{\textcolor{#D9730D}{\phi(q_t)^\top S_t} \;+\; \textcolor{#2E6DB4}{\sum_{j\in R(t)} \exp(q_t^\top k_j)\,f_{j:t}\,v_j}} {\textcolor{#D9730D}{\phi(q_t)^\top z_t} \;+\; \textcolor{#2E6DB4}{\sum_{j\in R(t)} \exp(q_t^\top k_j)\,f_{j:t}}}. \tag{1}\label{eq:routed}\]

Once the router has decided, the linear and softmax parts are independent and meet only in the shared denominator. Because routing colors whole columns, the readout splits exactly into a packed problem over the retained keys and a recurrent problem over the rest (routing \(r=[1,0,1,0,0]\); the shared normalizer is left out):

Each branch therefore gets its own kernel, which returns a normalized output together with its log-mass, and a cheap final step merges the two.

Packing moves keys, but it must not move time. In the packed term above, \(k_1\) and \(k_3\) sit side by side, yet \(q_5\)’s score against \(k_3\) still carries \(f_{3:5}\) (the gates of tokens 4 and 5, which went to the recurrent state). If we treated the packed keys as positions 1 and 2, those gates would vanish and the decay would be wrong. So every retained key keeps its original position, and the computation follows the routed output \(\eqref{eq:routed}\) exactly.

Calculating the Output

We start from the end: before opening up either kernel, here is what each one must return, and how the two results become the final output. Each branch divides its part of \(\eqref{eq:routed}\) by its own denominator, which we call its mass:

\[o^{\text{lin}}_t = \frac{\phi(q_t)^\top S_t}{z^{\text{lin}}_t}, \qquad z^{\text{lin}}_t = \phi(q_t)^\top z_t,\] \[o^{\text{exp}}_t = \frac{\sum_{j\in R(t)} \exp(q_t^\top k_j)\,f_{j:t}\,v_j}{z^{\text{exp}}_t}, \qquad z^{\text{exp}}_t = \sum_{j\in R(t)} \exp(q_t^\top k_j)\,f_{j:t}.\]

The final output is the average of the two, weighted by each branch’s share of the total mass: \(w^{\text{lin}}_t = z^{\text{lin}}_t / (z^{\text{lin}}_t + z^{\text{exp}}_t)\), \(w^{\text{exp}}_t = 1 - w^{\text{lin}}_t\), and \(o_t = w^{\text{lin}}_t\,o^{\text{lin}}_t + w^{\text{exp}}_t\,o^{\text{exp}}_t\). This is exactly \(\eqref{eq:routed}\).

Computing these masses directly is the problem. Their scales are extreme and very different: an exponential score overflows float32 once its logit passes about 88, while linear sums are scaled by products of forget gates that shrink toward zero. So each branch returns the logarithm of its mass instead, and the weights become a softmax that only ever exponentiates differences of log-masses, which are never positive:

\[\left(w^{\text{lin}}_t, w^{\text{exp}}_t\right) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\log z^{\text{lin}}_t,\ \log z^{\text{exp}}_t\right).\]

In the kernels, this two-way softmax is computed as \(o_t = o^{\text{dom}}_t + \sigma(\Delta_t)\,\big(o^{\text{other}}_t - o^{\text{dom}}_t\big)\), where “dom” is the branch with the larger log-mass and \(\Delta_t \le 0\) is the gap between the two: the output starts at the dominant branch and moves toward the other by exactly its share, and the only exponential is \(e^{\Delta_t}\le 1\). A branch with no keys has log-mass \(-\infty\) and gets zero weight. “A log-space state” below shows how the linear branch keeps its state this way.

Exponential Branch: Packed Attention

The exponential branch computes softmax attention over the retained keys only, about 10% of the sequence in our experiments. Doing that fast takes two steps. First, we pack the retained keys into a contiguous buffer. Each key keeps its original position, which the attention computation needs for decay and causality. Then a FlashAttention-style kernel splits the queries and packed keys into blocks and processes the score matrix one tile (a query block × a key block) at a time. Because packing keeps the keys in order, the usual causal-attention shortcuts still apply: tiles entirely in the future are skipped, and only tiles crossing the causal frontier need a mask. The only difference is that the frontier now follows the routing rather than the diagonal.

Packing the retained keys

Once the retained keys are packed, the pairwise work scales with \(\lvert R\rvert\) rather than \(T\). Packing is one prefix scan over the routing mask plus a scatter, per KV group. Each packed slot \(n\) keeps its key, value, and original position \(p_n\), the position the rule above asks for. The scan also gives each query its causal frontier \(c(t)\), the number of retained keys at or before \(t\). All query heads in a KV group share the packed buffer.

# per KV group, 0-based slots; simplified
c = cumsum(r)               # c[t]: causal frontier of query t
for j in where(r == 1):     # in parallel; original order is preserved
    n = c[j] - 1            # slot of key j
    K_pack[n], V_pack[n] = k[j], v[j]
    p[n] = j                # original position
    L_pack[n] = L[j]        # cumulative log-forget at j (used below)

Attention over packed tiles

Within each tile, the kernel runs an online softmax as in FlashAttention. Following FoX, decay enters as a logit offset. With the cumulative log-forget \(L(t)=\sum_{u\le t}\log f_u\), so that \(f_{j:t}=\exp\big(L(t)-L(j)\big)\):

\[s_{tn} = q_t^\top k_{p_n} + L(t) - L(p_n).\]

Storing \(L(p_n)\) at packing time makes the gaps between retained keys free: a key 1,000 positions back simply gets more decay. Without routing (\(r\equiv1\)), \(p_n=n\) and this is exactly forgetting attention.

As in causal FlashAttention, there are three kinds of tiles, and they still work here because the packed keys stay sorted by position:

  • future tiles, where every packed key lies after every query in the tile, are skipped entirely;
  • interior tiles, where every key is before every query, are fully causal and need no per-pair comparison;
  • only boundary tiles need a causal mask.

Play with the routing mask and watch the tiles:

In the kernel, interior and boundary tiles run in two separate loops, so interior tiles carry no masking logic; the if below expresses that split compactly:

# one program per (query head, query tile I); simplified, 0-based slots
n = c[I]                                    # causal frontier of each query row
m, l, acc = -inf, 0.0, 0.0                  # online-softmax state, FP32
for J in key_tiles:                         # packed slots, in order
    if J.first >= max(n): break             # future tile: skip the rest
    s = q[I] @ K_pack[J].T + L[I][:, None] - L_pack[J][None, :]
    if J.last >= min(n):                    # boundary tile only
        s[J[None, :] >= n[:, None]] = -inf  # past each row's frontier
    m, l, acc = online_softmax(m, l, acc, s, V_pack[J])
o_exp, logz_exp = acc / l, m + log(l)       # (0, -inf) if no keys

The kernel returns its normalized output and log-mass for the merge.

Linear Branch: Log-Space Chunked Recurrence

The linear branch computes linear attention over the remaining keys, about 90% of the sequence in our experiments. With so many keys, packing would save little, so we mask out the keys that went to the KV cache instead and run a chunked recurrence over the whole sequence, as in GLA and Mamba-2. What changes is how the state is stored: as a normalized mean and a log-mass rather than raw sums. The reason is that both branches share one denominator, and exponential scores can be huge or tiny: raw linear sums would have to follow them to that scale, while a normalized output plus a log-mass can be merged at any scale.

Masking out KV-cache keys

We run the chunked recurrence over the entire sequence, with no metadata at all. Keys that went to the KV cache are removed from this branch by masking their key contribution inside the kernel, while keeping their forget gates:

\[\log\widetilde\phi(k_j)_d = \begin{cases} \log\phi(k_j)_d, & r_j = 0,\\ -\infty, & r_j = 1. \end{cases}\]

After exponentiation the masked keys get weight \(e^{-\infty}=0\), so the feature–value update \(\widetilde\phi(k_j)v_j^\top\) vanishes without touching \(v_j\). Queries stay dense, because every position reads the linear history. The result is an ordinary gated linear-attention recurrence over a contiguous sequence, with no gap-aware indexing. Keeping the gates is the same time-indexing rule as before: the decay between two compressed tokens still includes the gates of any retained tokens between them.

A log-space state

Why not just keep the raw numerator \(S\) and denominator \(z\)? Three attempts show the problem, all in float32:

  1. Raw sums. Keep \(S\) and \(z\), and the softmax scores \(\exp(q_t^\top k_j)\) beside them in the shared denominator of \(\eqref{eq:routed}\). Any logit above about 88 already makes \(\exp\) overflow to \(\infty\).
  2. Rescale by the softmax maximum \(m\), as FlashAttention does. The exponential side is now fine, but the linear sums are scaled by the same \(e^{-m}\): with \(m=110\), a linear mass of 1 becomes exactly 0, and the linear branch silently disappears. Long contexts cause the same problem on their own: ten thousand gates of 0.99 multiply to about \(10^{-44}\).
  3. Store means and log-masses. For each feature \(d\), keep the normalized value mean \(\bar V_d = S_d / z_d\) and the log-mass \(\log z_d\). The mean always stays within the range of the values, and every scale lives in a log, where \(e^{-110}\) is just \(-110\).

Storing log-masses also gives the branch output a log-mass, which the final merge with the exponential branch needs. Every stage of the kernel, and the decode step, is built from one primitive, merge, which combines normalized values with log-masses; we show it next to the reference code below.

Chunked prefill in three stages

Prefill splits the sequence into chunks of 64 tokens and runs three stages, following chunked GLA but in log space, with every step written as a merge.

Here is the whole branch as a minimal PyTorch reference for one head (with F = torch.nn.functional and inf = float("inf")). It is laid out like the kernels and matches the direct formula to float64 precision. Every step combines (mean, log-mass) pairs with one primitive, merge.

In one line, merge is attention over its entries, with the log-masses as logits: a softmax-weighted average of the values, plus the log-sum-exp of the log-masses,

\[\operatorname{merge}(x, a) = \big(\operatorname{softmax}(a)^\top x,\ \operatorname{logsumexp}(a)\big).\]

PyTorch’s softmax and log-sum-exp already subtract the maximum internally, the same trick as online softmax. The only extra step is an empty input, where every log-mass is \(-\infty\): softmax would return NaN, which would then spread through the scan, so we map it to zero weights.

Code: merge 
def merge(x, a):
    """Merge normalized values x[..., n, :] with log-masses a[..., n]."""
    p = a.softmax(-1).nan_to_num()          # empty input (all -inf) -> 0
    return (p[..., None] * x).sum(-2), a.logsumexp(-1)

merge is averaging averages: to combine the average grades of two classes, weight each class’s average by its size. It does exactly that, with the sizes kept as logarithms so they can be astronomically large or small. Because the output is a convex combination, the mean always stays within the range of its inputs, and all scale information lives in a single log-mass. The kernels keep this exact even in BF16: a weighted average of identical values should return exactly that value, but the weights are rounded before the matrix product and no longer sum to one. So they normalize by the sum of the rounded weights and center the values on an anchor, and a query that sees a single key returns that key’s value directly.

The branch itself is four calls: a setup step, then one per row of the figure:

def linear_branch(lq, lk, v, r, logf, C=64):
    """lq, lk: log phi(q), log phi(k) [T, D]; v: [T, Dv];
    r: 1 if the key went to the KV cache [T]; logf: log gates [T]."""
    T = lq.shape[0]
    lq, lk, v, L = prepare_chunks(lq, lk, v, r, logf, C)  # 0. setup
    s, Vloc, zloc = local_step(lq, lk, v, L)    # 1. parallel
    Vin, zin = scan_step(Vloc, zloc, L)         # 2. sequential
    o, z = readout_step(lq, v, s, Vin, zin, L)  # 3. parallel
    return o.flatten(0, 1)[:T], z.flatten(0, 1)[:T]

0. Preparing the chunks. Keys the router sent to the KV cache get log-feature \(-\infty\) here, so they drop out of the linear branch, while their gates stay in logf. The sequence is padded to whole chunks, and decay is kept within each chunk: L restarts at every chunk boundary, as in GLA’s chunkwise kernels.

Code: prepare_chunks 
def prepare_chunks(lq, lk, v, r, logf, C):
    """Mask KV-cache keys, pad to whole chunks, reshape to [N, C, ...]."""
    lk = lk.masked_fill(r[:, None], -inf)   # mask keys, keep their gates
    P = -lq.shape[0] % C
    lq, lk = F.pad(lq, (0, 0, 0, P)), F.pad(lk, (0, 0, 0, P), value=-inf)
    v, logf = F.pad(v, (0, 0, 0, P)), F.pad(logf, (0, P))
    N = lq.shape[0] // C
    L = logf.view(N, C).cumsum(-1)          # log-forget within each chunk
    return lq.view(N, C, -1), lk.view(N, C, -1), v.view(N, C, -1), L

1. Local step (parallel over chunks). Each chunk scores its queries against its own keys, \(s_{tj}\) \(= \operatorname{logsumexp}_d\big(\log\phi(q_t)_d + \log\widetilde\phi(k_j)_d\big) + L(t) - L(j)\), and summarizes its keys into one (mean, log-mass) pair per feature \(d\), decayed to the chunk’s end.

In the kernel, this log-sum-exp is a single tensor-core matrix product. The decay is folded into the features around a reference position, as in GLA’s secondary chunking. Each key feature is then shifted by its maximum over the tile (and that maximum added to the queries instead), and each query row by its own maximum. Now every exponent is at most zero, so the exponentiated queries and keys can be multiplied as an ordinary matrix product; taking the log and adding the query shift back gives \(s_{tj}\) exactly. The reference code computes the log-sum-exp directly, for clarity.

Code: local_step 
def local_step(lq, lk, v, L):
    """Causal scores s_tj inside each chunk, and each chunk's summary."""
    s = torch.logsumexp(lq[:, :, None] + lk[:, None], -1)
    s = s + L[:, :, None] - L[:, None, :]   # decay from key j to query t
    C = s.shape[-1]
    s = s.masked_fill(~torch.ones(C, C, dtype=torch.bool).tril(), -inf)
    to_end = (L[:, -1:] - L)[..., None]     # decay from key j to the end
    Vloc, zloc = merge(v[:, None], (lk + to_end).transpose(1, 2))
    return s, Vloc, zloc                    # Vloc: [N, D, Dv]

2. Scan (the only loop). The state is carried from chunk to chunk: decay it across the chunk, then merge in that chunk’s summary. The loop runs over \(T/64\) chunks rather than \(T\) tokens, and records the state each chunk starts from.

Code: scan_step 
def scan_step(Vloc, zloc, L):
    """Carry the state across chunks; return each incoming state."""
    Vbar, logz = torch.zeros_like(Vloc[0]), torch.full_like(zloc[0], -inf)
    Vin, zin = [], []
    for c in range(len(Vloc)):
        Vin.append(Vbar); zin.append(logz)
        Vbar, logz = merge(torch.stack([Vbar, Vloc[c]], 1),
                           torch.stack([logz + L[c, -1], zloc[c]], -1))
    return torch.stack(Vin), torch.stack(zin)

3. Readout (parallel over chunks). Each query merges the state its chunk started from, one entry per feature \(d\) weighted by \(\phi(q_t)_d\) and decayed to \(t\), with its own chunk’s keys.

Code: readout_step 
def readout_step(lq, v, s, Vin, zin, L):
    """Each query merges its incoming state with its chunk's keys."""
    eta = lq + zin[:, None] + L[..., None]   # one entry per feature d
    return merge(torch.cat([Vin, v], 1)[:, None], torch.cat([eta, s], -1))

Steps 1 and 3 are dense matrix products, which is what makes chunking fast on tensor cores. The full equations are in Appendix C.5 of the paper.

Train / Prefill

Training adds two things to prefill: a backward pass through both kernels, and the router’s loss. It stays cheap for the same reason prefill does: only the retained keys are compared pairwise, so at about 10% retention the exponential branch does about a tenth of full attention’s pairwise work, and the linear branch stays linear in \(T\) (Section 4.5 of the paper gives the full count).

Measured on one H100 with the 2B models at batch 1, against full FlashAttention and the GLA 1:4 hybrid (the faster of our two hybrid families): on short prompts attention is a small share of the cost and FlashAttention’s kernels win, but past 8K tokens the pairwise work Ark skips takes over, and at 64K Ark prefills 2.6× faster than full attention and 1.17× faster than the hybrid.

Backward pass. Both kernels follow the FlashAttention pattern of saving little and recomputing the rest. The packed kernel keeps only each query’s row maximum and normalizer, and rebuilds the attention weights from them. The linear kernel keeps its chunk boundary states. Because the final merge is fused into it, it also receives the exponential branch’s output and log-mass, so it can differentiate through that merge.

The original positions earn their keep again here. Decay enters each score as \(L(t) - L(p_n)\), so the gradient for \(L\) has a key-side part at every packed key. The kernel scatters it back to the key’s original position \(p_n\), and the gate gradients then follow from \(L\), which is just a running sum of log-gates. Routing decisions are hard and carry no gradient, so the language-model loss never reaches the router.

The router’s loss. The router learns only from its own loss from Part 1, a KL divergence between the softmax teacher \(p\) and the routed mixture \(m/Z\), estimated from about ten queries per sequence rather than all \(T\). The KL splits as

\[\mathrm{KL}\big(p \,\|\, m/Z\big) = \sum_j p_j\,(\log p_j - \log m_j) + \log Z,\]

so one pass over the keys gives the two branch normalizers, and a second accumulates both the KL and \(\log Z\) on the fly, together with the router’s compression count for the budget. Nothing is stored for backward: the narrow scores are recomputed.

Decode

At decode time the router looks at each new token once and sends it to one memory:

  • Compressed (\(r_t=0\)): merge it into the recurrent state; the KV cache is untouched.
  • Retained (\(r_t=1\)): append it to the KV cache, with its position and \(L(t)\). The recurrent state only decays.

The retained case is where the log-space state pays off again. Decaying the state multiplies its numerator and denominator by the same gate, \(S_t = f_tS_{t-1}\) and \(z_t = f_tz_{t-1}\), so their ratio, the stored mean, does not change; only the log-mass moves:

\[\bar V_{t,d} = \frac{S_{t,d}}{z_{t,d}} = \frac{f_tS_{t-1,d}}{f_tz_{t-1,d}} = \bar V_{t-1,d}, \qquad \log z_{t,d} = \log z_{t-1,d} + \log f_t .\]

A retained step never touches the \(d_k \times d_v\) mean matrix, only \(d_k\) numbers.

Each step then reads the state and the retained entries instead of every past entry. Counting attention memory alone, with the access-count model in Section 4.5 of the paper (derived in Appendix C.7), that beats full attention from about 136 tokens of context on, and is about ten times cheaper at long context. How much of that reaches end-to-end speed? Every step also streams all the model weights once, shared by the batch, and that cost does not shrink. Extending the same count with the weights, for the 2B models at 64K context and batch 8 (BF16 weights and KV cache, FP32 state):

Per decode step Weights Attention memory (8 requests) Total
Full attention 4.2 GB 30.1 GB 34.3 GB
Ark 4.5 GB 3.2 GB 7.7 GB

The attention memory shrinks about 9.5×, but the total only about 4.4×, close to the measured 3.35×; the rest goes to kernels that don’t reach peak bandwidth, launches and compute. At batch 1 the same count gives only about 1.6×, and larger batches push it toward 9.5×.

The measurement, on one H100 at batch 8: with a 4K prompt, Ark decodes faster than both baselines at every generation length, and the gap widens as the output grows, reaching 3.0× over full FlashAttention and 1.6× over the GLA 1:4 hybrid after 64K generated tokens. With a growing prompt instead (256 generated tokens, the other tab), it reaches 3.35× and 1.60× at 64K.

The cache. The KV cache is a preallocated buffer that each request fills as tokens are retained, and every step reads only the filled part, about a tenth of it; that is where the decode speedup comes from. A growing or paged cache would turn the same saving into a smaller memory footprint too, at a small cost each time the cache grows.

Conclusion

Making Ark fast came down to respecting one asymmetry, one rule and one primitive:

  • pack the few retained keys and run tiled softmax over them, mask the many compressed ones and run a log-space chunked recurrence;
  • packing moves keys, not time: every retained key keeps its original position, so the split is exact and both branches share one decay;
  • keep every total as a log-mass, so one merge combines chunks, states and branches at any scale.

Together they give exact routed attention at a fraction of the pairwise work, and a decode step that reads a fixed-size state plus about a tenth of the KV cache: 3.35× faster than FlashAttention and 1.60× faster than a GLA hybrid at 64K.

Closing the Series

Over three posts, we followed one idea: not every token needs softmax.

  • Part 1 made the kernel choice per entry: a learned router sends each token, in each KV group of each layer, either to a KV cache read through softmax or to a recurrent state read through linear attention, and learns from a softmax teacher.
  • Part 2 showed that it pays off in quality per stored element: recall on par with hybrids that store 25–33% more, a learned choice of what to keep that beats eviction at equal memory, and retrieval that runs through the few cached entries.
  • Part 3 made it fast: packed attention for the few cached keys, a log-space chunked recurrence for the rest, and one merge that ties them together.

Each piece leaves room to grow. A router that could revisit its decisions would need the decode cache to promote entries from the recurrent state back into the KV cache. A budget that adapts to the input would let each request fill a different share of that cache. And because the two branches only meet through (output, log-mass) pairs, a richer recurrence such as the delta rule could replace the linear branch without changing the exponential side. Building on Ark? We’d love to hear about that!

entry.title: Raven (Part-2)
entry.content:
This post is cross-posted at Goomblab Blog.
Raven Series  —  ← Part 1: Memory as a set of Slots  |  Part 2: Architecture and Results

From Framework to Model

In Part 1, we introduced Routing Slot Memories (RSM), a framework that combines the selective writing of SWA with the gradual forgetting of SSMs. The next step was to turn that framework into a concrete model.

RSM is deliberately general. To instantiate Raven, one needs to choose how the router $r_t$ is computed and how the decay term $a_t$ is parameterized. We wanted a design expressive enough to learn meaningful slot assignments, but simple enough to train stably at scale.

Our recurrence uses separate key and value states, mirroring SWA, but replaces hard deletion with learned decay:

$$ S^k_t = (1-\exp(a_tr_t)) \odot S^k_{t-1} + \exp(a_tr_t)^\top k_t $$ $$ S^v_t = (1-\exp(a_tr_t)) \odot S^v_{t-1} + \exp(a_tr_t)^\top v_t $$

Unlike standard SSMs that write to all memory slots at once ($r_t = \mathbf{1}$), Raven writes only to the slots selected by $r_t$. And unlike SWA, which fully overwrites the evicted slot, Raven decays the previous content of the selected slot rather than removing it outright.

For routing, we draw inspiration from the DeepSeek Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) family . Each token is projected to a score vector, and only the top-$K$ entries remain active:

$$ \begin{aligned} m_t &= \sigma(Wx_t), \\ g_t &= \mathrm{KeepTop}_K(m_t) = \begin{cases} m_t[i], & \text{if } i \in \mathrm{TopK}(m_t),\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$

By isolating only the highest-scoring slots, the memory dynamically specializes based on the content of the token. Finally, to keep the effective write magnitude stable, these gated scores are normalized into the final routing weights:

$$ r_t = \frac{g_t}{\alpha\sum_{i=1}^M g_t[i]}. $$

Here, $\alpha$ controls the effective write scale, similarly to the role of temperature-like scaling in GLA , we used $\alpha=1$ for 400M model size and $\alpha=4$ for 800M model size.

Design Decisions

With the recurrence fixed, we turned to the block design.

Dropping the short convolution. Most linear transformer blocks include a short depthwise convolution before the recurrence — a holdover that helps capture local context. We removed it. The reasoning: SWA is mathematically equivalent to an input-dependent convolution, and Raven’s RSM already subsumes SWA as a special case. Adding a separate convolution on top would be redundant.

On norms. Following common practice in both Transformers and linear attention/SSMs, we apply QK-RMSNorm to queries and keys to stabilize training and avoid gradient explosions, following common practice in SSMs. One interesting exception appears in hybrid Raven, where Raven layers are interleaved with attention. In that setting, removing these norms improves length generalization, especially on recall tasks. We hypothesize that the norms suppress position-related information that the NoPE attention layers rely on. This was one of the more unexpected ablation results.

Side Note on RoPE

In early experiments, we applied Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) to queries and keys. This substantially hurt Raven’s length generalization, which is one of its main strengths, so we removed it from the final design.

No load balancing. In Mixture-of-Experts models, load-balancing losses are commonly used to spread tokens more evenly across experts. We do not use such a loss in Raven, since its memory is most useful when allocation is uneven. Slots that specialize in retrieval-critical tokens, such as passkeys, variable names, or rare facts, should receive more of those tokens rather than be pushed toward uniform usage. For this reason, we allow the router to specialize freely, and use Gumbel noise during training only to encourage exploration and avoid early collapse. This intuition is supported by our experiments: retrieval-critical tokens naturally cluster into dedicated slots, while other slots remain available for ordinary context.

Empirical Results

We now turn to the empirical evaluation. Our main question was whether Raven improves in-context retrieval without sacrificing general language modeling.

Retrieval Ability

We begin with retrieval. We compare Raven against Mamba-2 , GDN , and GLA on the SSM side, and SWA-like models including SWA+RoPE and GSA on the other — and threw Needle-in-a-Haystack tasks at all of them.

The baseline behavior is consistent with their memory mechanism: Mamba-2 and GDN write every token to every slot, so over a long sequence, each slot becomes a blurry average of everything it has ever seen. By 8K tokens — already $4\times$ their training length — the passkey signal is too diluted to recover.

Table 2: In-context recall benchmarks and NIAH accuracy vs. context length and cache size. We report accuracy (%) on SWDE/FDA/SQuAD and on single NIAH-1/2/3 across context lengths. Rec. mem. and Conv. mem. denote the millions of cached state elements used during decoding. The common baseline of \(12.5M\) recurrent elements corresponds to a 24-layer model with a total state size of \(0.57M\) per layer (derived from \(2\times\) factors in architectures like GSA/SWA or larger single tensors in Mamba-2/GDN).

Raven behaved differently. It held near-perfect accuracy ($\geq \mathbf{99\%}$) all the way to 16K tokens, and remained the only model at the 400M scale to keep strong performance ($> \mathbf{91\%}$) at 32K — that’s $\mathbf{16\times}$ its training length.
In contrast, Raven is dramatically better at NIAH-1 than all other models.
This behavior is consistent with the routing mechanism: the passkey can be written into a dedicated slot and remain recoverable over long spans, rather than being diluted by subsequent tokens.

Language Modeling

A natural question is whether this improvement in retrieval comes at the expense of general language modeling. We had deliberately made the memory uneven — would that hurt perplexity or zero-shot benchmarks?

Across standard evaluations, Raven matched or surpassed Mamba-2 , GLA , and GDN , as well as strong Transformer baselines like FoX, at both 400M and 800M parameter scales. It even achieved the best Lambada performance at 400M. These results suggest that selective memory does not compromise general language modeling, and may even help by routing tokens to more appropriate slots.

Table 3: Language modeling and zero-shot evaluation results. Perplexity on Lambada (LMB.) and zero-shot accuracy on Lambada, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, and ARC-c for Transformer, SSM, and Raven models at 400M and 800M parameter scales. Raven matches strong linear baselines overall while maintaining strong downstream performance.

Hybrid Raven

We also experimented with a hybrid variant — interleaving Raven RSM layers with standard attention layers. The results here were striking. The hybrid Raven achieved near-perfect NIAH-1 accuracy up to 32K tokens and strong NIAH-2 performance up to 16K tokens, while other SSM hybrids like GDN+Attn and Mamba-2+Attn started breaking down at 4K and 2K respectively. The combination of NoPE attention — good at precise short-range retrieval — with Raven’s persistent, content-addressed slots turned out to be unusually complementary.

Table 4: Hybrid Models Retrieval Ability. Recall ability of hybrid-raven vs other hybrid architechtures.

In the 800M hybrid setting, Raven is the best model for in-context recall and length extrapolation — while GDN and SWA+RoPE drop to 0% accuracy beyond their training length, Raven retains around 80% accuracy on NIAH-2 at 64K tokens, which is 16× its training sequence length.

Length Generalization

One surprising outcome was Raven’s strong length generalization. During evaluation, we found that Raven remained effective far beyond its training length, beyond what had previously been observed in SSM-based models. This behavior was not explicitly designed for, which motivated us to look for a mechanistic explanation. In developing that explanation, we found it useful to think in terms of Effective Sequence Length (ESL) (ESL), a concept that came out of our discussion with Ricardo.

Figure: Effective Sequence Length. Normalized effective sequence length for a NIAH-1 sample at sequence length 16K. SWA stores each token in exactly one slot (FIFO). Raven shows the hidden state $S_t$ for layer 1, head 1 (256 slots, Top$_{32}$). SSM stores each token in all slots with decay. Slots are reordered by usage frequency; results correspond to 400M parameter models.

In a standard SSM, every slot receives every token, so the effective sequence length of each slot is $T$. In SWA, each slot receives exactly $\frac{T}{M}$ tokens, yielding uniform allocation across slots. In Raven, routing produces a more heterogeneous pattern: some slots receive many tokens, while others receive only a small subset, including rare retrieval-critical tokens. As a result, different slots operate over different effective sequence lengths, which may help explain Raven’s improved length generalization.

To make this concrete, we visualize Raven’s hidden state on a synthetic NIAH task:

Figure: Raven Memory Dynamics — Layer 23, Head 4. The box is Raven's recurrent memory: 512 slots arranged left-to-right, each displayed as a vertical line. The memory starts completely empty (gray) and fills token by token as the prompt is processed. ▮ Red slots are claimed by the passkey tokens (RecallSSM1378) — the router directs them into a dedicated region and keeps them there. ▮ Blue slots receive both passkey and context writes and act as shared memory. ▮ Green slots absorb the surrounding context tokens only. Brightness grows each time a slot is revisited — darker means written once, fully saturated means written many times. When Raven: begins generating the answer, it reads from the red region and the retrieval slots brighten further, showing the model recovering exactly what it stored.

The passkey — shown in $\color{red}{red}$ — is routed into a dedicated region of the hidden state and remains separated from most ordinary tokens. Ordinary tokens shown in $\color{green}{green}$ flow through the general-purpose slots without touching it. Some slots shown in $\color{blue}{blue}$ serve both roles. Crucially, different heads allocate different amounts of memory to retrieval-critical tokens — the model discovered this specialization entirely on its own, without any explicit supervision.

This is what “organizing memory like a closet” looks like from the inside.

Final Notes and Future

Raven began from a simple goal: improving recall in linear models. More broadly, it suggests that learned memory can benefit from structured, content-based allocation rather than uniform updates across slots. In Raven, a relatively simple routing mechanism is enough to improve recall while remaining competitive on language modeling, with the additional benefit of strong length generalization.

There is plenty left to explore. How far can the length generalization be pushed? Can the routing mechanism be made even more expressive? What happens at truly large scales? We don’t have all the answers yet — but we’re working on it.

entry.title: Raven (Part-1)
entry.content:
This post is cross-posted at Goomblab Blog.
Raven Series  —  Part 1: Memory as a set of Slots  |  Part 2: Architecture and Results →

🐦‍⬛ Ravens are among the most intelligent birds known — famous for caching food across hundreds of locations and retrieving each item with remarkable precision. Just like our new model, which stores information selectively and can retrieve it cleanly when needed!

The Recall Gap

Mamba showed that attention is not strictly necessary for strong language modeling. A simple recurrent model could match, and sometimes outperform, Transformers on language modeling at a fraction of the cost. But there is no free lunch. Soon after, several works exposed a critical limitation: fixed-size memory models struggle on recall benchmarks, which is not surprising, since they have only a finite amount of room to store information. While it’s tempting to blame their finite capacity, the reality is more nuanced.

Consider Needle-In-The-Haystack (NIAH). The model is first given a lookup key, then a long dictionary, and finally asked to retrieve the matching value. This is a form of constant-memory recall: in principle, it requires only $O(1)$ memory, since the model only needs to retain the key and its corresponding value as it scans the sequence (unlike scaling-memory recall tasks like KV-Retrieval, which require $O(T)$ memory because the query comes after the dictionary).

Despite this theoretical $O(1)$ requirement, recurrent models still lag behind Transformers on NIAH. This failure isn’t just a quirk of synthetic benchmarks; it mirrors real-world bottlenecks. In multiple-choice questions, a recurrent model may identify the correct answer early on but fail to preserve that single letter in its state until the output . Similarly, in math and code, recurrent models struggle to track a single variable or a few intermediate values over long distances.

The problem is not a lack of space: the model has enough capacity to store the information. Rather, it lacks the structure needed to organize its state, so new data interferes with what is already stored instead of maintaining its persistence.

From Global States to Partitioned Slots 👕

Can we design a recurrent model with strong constant-memory recall that approaches theoretical limits?

To build intuition, think of the hidden state as a closet. Good organization is not just about how much space you have, but about how that space is structured. When a new item arrives, you usually do two things:

1. Choose where it should go. (Routing)
2. Clear just enough space there to fit it. (Squeezing / Decay)

Memory in recurrent models faces the same dual requirement. A model should decide which part of its state should store the new information, and it should update that part without unnecessarily altering the rest. This motivates the idea of slots: subsets of the hidden state that can be updated independently. With this structure, a new token can modify only the relevant slot(s), while other stored information remains undisturbed.

SSMs write blindly and decay uniformly

State space models (SSMs) and linear attention all share the same fundamental memory operation — a matrix-valued hidden state $S_t \in \mathbb{R}^{M\times d}$ updated by a linear time-dependent recurrence:

\[S_t = \underbrace{S_{t-1}A_t}_{\text{Decay}} + \underbrace{v_t k_t^\top}_{\text{Write}}, \qquad o_t = \underbrace{S_t q_t}_{\text{Read}}\]

SSMs are strong at the reorganization step. The forget gate $A_t$ decays old content to make room for new information. But they do not control where information is written.

In the diagonal case ($A_t=\text{diag}(a_t)$), the update simplifies to $S_t = S_{t-1} \odot a_t + v_t k_t^\top$. Here, the scalar $a_t$ applies uniform decay across the entire state. Because the write $v_t k_t^\top$ lands across all $M$ rows, every new token perturbs everything already stored. There is little isolation between memory contents, so interference accumulates.

SWA writes precisely but forcefully evicts

Sliding window attention (SWA) takes the opposite approach. It maintains a fixed cache and, at each step, $\color{red}{\text{drops}}$ the oldest token to $\color{green}{\text{append}}$ the newest one. Written as a matrix update using a one-hot selector $e_t$:

\[[S^{k}_t, S^v_t] = \underbrace{(\mathbf{1} - e_t)}_{\color{red}{\text{Remove oldest}}}\odot[S^{k}_{t-1}, S^v_{t-1}] + \underbrace{e_t}_{\color{green}{\text{Write new}}} [k_t^\top, v_t^\top]\]

SWA is precise about where it writes: it updates exactly one slot ($e_t$). But it doesn’t reorganize memory well. Instead of compressing or preserving old content, it removes entries outright to make room for new ones.

The Dual Requirement

SSMs and SWA fail in complementary ways. SSMs update memory too diffusely; SWA updates memory too rigidly.

Bridging the recall gap requires a mechanism that can do both: treat subsets of the hidden state as independent slots, and decide which ones should be updated versus preserved. This dual requirement—routing and decay—is the foundation of our framework.

Routing Slot Memories (RSM)

Bridging the gap between “blind writes” and “forced eviction” requires a unifying framework. Instead of writing everywhere (SSM) or writing to a fixed rotation (SWA), an RSM uses a learned sparse router $r_t \in \mathbb{R}^M$.

This router looks at the current token and determines which slots should change and which should remain untouched:

\[S_t = \underbrace{(\mathbf{1} - r_t) \odot S_{t-1}}_{\text{Persistence}} + \underbrace{r_t \odot \bigl(D_t\,S_{t-1}\,A_t + U_t\bigr)}_{\text{Selective Update}}\]

By making $r_t$ sparse, the RSM treats the state as a collection of independent subspaces:

  • The Persistence Term: If the router does not select a slot ($r_t = 0$), that memory remains mathematically identical to the previous step. It is “shielded.”
  • The Update Term: Only the “active” slots undergo the decay ($D_t, A_t$) and write ($U_t$) process.

By simply changing the behavior of the router $r_t$, this single equation provides a unified view of several prominent sequence model families:

A dense router ($r_t = \mathbf{1}$) recovers an SSM, where every token updates the full state. A one-hot cyclic router ($r_t = e_t$) recovers SWA, where each token updates a single slot in a fixed rotation.

The question then becomes concrete: can a model learn, purely from data, which slot each token should occupy, and preserve that assignment over time?

Our answer is Raven. By using a learned sparse router, Raven treats its hidden state like a Mixture-of-Experts for memory. It can place critical information into dedicated slots and avoid corrupting those slots with irrelevant filler tokens.

In Part 2, we’ll move from theory to practice: we’ll look at the specific architecture of the Raven block, the “counterintuitive” design decisions that made it work, and how this organized memory allows it to recall information $16\times$ beyond its training length.
